name: Testing Arguments Before Peer Review
title: Testing Arguments Before Peer Review
answer: Testing arguments before peer review means using structured critique to find weak premises, unsupported claims, alternative explanations, and logical gaps in a manuscript before submitting to a journal. It covers empirical claims, theoretical inferences, and policy or practice recommendations. The goal is to reduce desk rejection and reviewer friction by surfacing objections early. This work sits between drafting and formal submission, and it applies to single-author papers, collaborative projects, and grant proposals.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Testing arguments before peer review means using structured critique to find weak premises, unsupported claims, alternative explanations, and logical gaps in a manuscript before submitting to a journal. It covers empirical claims, theoretical inferences, and policy or practice recommendations. The goal is to reduce desk rejection and reviewer friction by surfacing objections early. This work sits between drafting and formal submission, and it applies to single-author papers, collaborative projects, and grant proposals.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of large language models, citation databases, and local document stores. A researcher typically uploads a manuscript or argument outline to a tool that can parse sections, extract claims, and compare them against a reference corpus. Some setups use retrieval augmented generation over open access papers, while others run entirely on local models to keep unpublished text private. The site's library of 135 research papers and 10,555 extracted claims can serve as a small benchmark for claim checking, but most practitioners bring their own field specific corpora.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method is iterative and adversarial. First, the author breaks the argument into discrete claims, each with its evidence and warrant. Then a model or checklist asks targeted questions: Is this claim supported by the cited source? What would falsify it? Are there confounding variables or selection effects? The author revises weak claims, adds missing caveats, or flags sections for a human colleague. Some workflows use multiple models with different prompting styles to avoid a single model's blind spots.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on confidentiality, authorship, and overreliance. Unpublished manuscripts are sensitive, so any cloud tool must have clear data handling terms, and many researchers prefer local or self hosted models. There is also a risk that an AI critique is confidently wrong, so a human must verify every suggested counterargument against the original source. Provenance matters: the site links to original papers rather than a secondary search tool, which helps authors trace a claim back to its evidence. No tool output should be treated as peer review itself.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where it is going is toward structured argument maps and reproducible critique logs. Future tools may attach a machine readable record of which claims were tested, what objections were raised, and how the author responded, so editors can see the pre review history. Models are also likely to improve at domain specific reasoning, such as checking statistical assumptions or clinical trial limitations, but they will remain a supplement to human judgment rather than a replacement for expert reviewers.
